data.summary:
Input: A 2D grid of characters and a target word string
Output: A boolean indicating whether the target word can be constructed by sequentially adjacent cells
Rules: The same grid cell may not be used more than once in a single path
constraints: board and word consists of only lowercase and uppercase English letters.

data.generator_code:
import random

def generate(rng, n):
    m = max(1, min(6, n))
    board = [[chr(rng.randint(65, 90)) for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    word_len = rng.randint(1, min(15, m * m))
    word = "".join(rng.choice([board[i][j] for i in range(m) for j in range(m)]) for _ in range(word_len))
    return [board, word]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    m = max(1, min(6, n))
    board = [["A" for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    word = "A" * min(15, m * m)
    return [board, word]

data.key_insight: We can explore every possible path starting from every cell in the grid that matches the first letter of the word. To ensure we don't reuse the same cell in a single path, we temporarily mark the cell as visited during the recursion and restore it upon backtracking.

steps.detail: Traverse every cell in the 2D grid. If a cell's character matches the first character of the word, start a backtracking search from that cell.

steps.title: Recursive backtracking function
steps.detail: Define a helper function that takes the current row, current column, and the index of the character we are trying to match in the word.

steps.title: Base cases
steps.detail: If the index reaches the length of the word, we have successfully matched all characters, so return True. If the current position is out of bounds or the cell character does not match the required character in the word, return False.

steps.title: Mark as visited and explore neighbors
steps.detail: Temporarily modify the current cell (e.g., set it to a special character like '#') to prevent revisiting it. Recursively search all four adjacent cells (up, down, left, right) for the next character.

steps.title: Restore cell and return result
steps.detail: After exploring all neighbors, restore the original character of the current cell (backtracking). Return True if any of the recursive neighbor searches succeed, otherwise False.

data.pattern_summary: Depth-First Search with backtracking explores all valid paths branch by branch, undoing choices when they lead to dead ends. Use it when you need to find a sequence of choices in a grid or graph that satisfies specific conditions.

pattern_options.name: Depth-First Search (Backtracking)
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We must explore paths step by step and step back when a cell does not match the next letter.

pattern_options.name: Sliding Window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding window applies to contiguous sequences in a 1D array, not 2D grid paths.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Paths cannot be easily broken down into independent overlapping subproblems because cells cannot be reused within the same path.

pattern_options.name: Breadth-First Search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. BFS tracks shortest paths level by level, whereas here we need to verify a specific deep sequence of adjacent cells.

signals.hint: Requires keeping track of visited cells during the traversal and undoing it when backing up.

data.brute_force_idea: Start a recursive search from every cell in the grid that matches the first letter of the word, checking all four possible directions for the next letter while keeping track of visited cells.
data.brute_force_why: N is the number of cells in the grid and L is the length of the word, with up to 4 branching directions at each step.
data.bottleneck: There is no wasted work or redundant subproblem to eliminate. Every path must be checked because any cell can potentially lead to a valid word.
bottleneck_hints: Consider whether knowing the solution at cell A helps you solve cell B without searching.
Think about how many possible branching paths exist from any given cell in the worst case.
Observe that because paths depend entirely on their specific sequence of unique cells, there are no overlapping subproblems to cache.

data.overview: The Word Search algorithm uses Depth-First Search with backtracking to find if a target word exists in a 2D grid of characters. It starts exploring from any cell matching the first letter and recursively checks adjacent cells while ensuring no cell is reused in the same path.
data.intuition: Imagine tracing a word in a word search puzzle with your pencil. You look at neighboring letters to spell the word step by step, and if you hit a dead end, you lift your pencil, step back, and try a different path.

pitfalls: Forgetting to backtrack by removing the cell from the visited set after recursion.
Not handling grid boundaries correctly, leading to IndexError.
Starting DFS from every cell without checking if the first letter matches, causing unnecessary overhead.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The optimized approach avoids recreating the visited set on every recursive call by using a single shared set across all paths and backtracking by removing the element upon return. Additionally, pruning the initial search loop by checking if the starting cell matches the first letter of the word reduces unnecessary recursion calls.

derivation.note: Base case check executes once per recursion frame.
Boundary and mismatch checks execute on every frame before branching.
Adds current coordinate to the shared visited set.
Branches into four directions recursively up to the length of the word L.
Removes current coordinate from the shared visited set during backtracking.
Nested loops iterate over every cell in the grid to find potential starting points.

data.time_summary: The outer loops run N * M times. For each cell that matches the first letter, the DFS function branches into 4 directions up to the length of the word L. This results in a worst-case time complexity of O(N * M * 4^L).
data.space_summary: The recursion stack and the shared visited set grow up to a depth equal to the length of the word L, resulting in O(L) space complexity.
data.takeaway: When searching for paths in a grid with state constraints, use a single shared tracking structure and backtrack by undoing modifications rather than copying states across recursive frames.
mistakes: Trying to mutate Python strings directly in the board grid, which raises a TypeError since strings are immutable.
Forgetting to undo the visited state change during backtracking, causing valid overlapping paths to fail.
Failing to prune starting cells that do not match the first letter of the target word.
